stats-plots-s1.title: Heating two masses of water
stats-plots-s1.text: Students heated 100 g and 200 g of water, each starting at 20 °C, on identical hot plates set to the same power, and recorded the temperature every minute.

stats-plots-s2.title: Breaking a polymer apart
stats-plots-s2.text: Two tubes each held 50 mg of the same polymer dissolved in water at 37 °C. An enzyme that speeds up hydrolysis of the polymer was added to one tube; the other got the same volume of water. Every 2 minutes a sample was tested for the mass of free monomers released.

items.q: Calculate the slope of the 100 g line between 0 and 5 minutes. Give your answer in °C per minute to one decimal place.

why.correct: Slope = change in y ÷ change in x = (50.1 − 20.0) °C ÷ (5 − 0) min = 30.1 ÷ 5 = 6.02, which rounds to 6.0 °C/min.

items.q: Estimate the temperature of the 100 g sample at 2.5 minutes by reading between the measured points. Give your answer in °C to the nearest whole degree.

why.correct: This is interpolation. At 2 min the 100 g sample was 32.1 °C and at 3 min 37.9 °C; halfway between is (32.1 + 37.9) ÷ 2 = 35.0 °C.

items.q: A student extends the 100 g line and predicts the water will be at 110 °C after 15 minutes. What is the best evaluation of this prediction?
options: It is unreliable: it extrapolates far past the data, and at normal air pressure liquid water stops warming near 100 °C as heat goes into boiling.
It is reliable, because the points lie on a straight line, and a straight line drawn through data continues at the same slope however far it is extended.
It is unreliable, because the slope should be measured from the 200 g line, which is the larger and more representative sample.
It is reliable, as long as the student uses the slope from the first minute alone, when the hot plate is coldest.

why.correct: Extrapolation assumes the pattern continues outside the measured range. Here it cannot: once water reaches its boiling point, added heat breaks hydrogen bonds to turn liquid into vapor, and the temperature levels off near 100 °C.
options: Correct: extrapolation beyond the data, and a physical limit at the boiling point.
Data only show the pattern over the measured range; nothing guarantees a line keeps going.
The 200 g line has its own slope; it does not describe the 100 g sample.
Picking one minute does not fix the problem of predicting far beyond the measured range.

items.q: The slope of the 200 g line is about half the slope of the 100 g line. Which explanation fits?
options: Both hot plates supply heat at the same pace, and twice the mass of water needs twice the heat to rise by each degree.
The 200 g water has a lower specific heat than the 100 g water, so each gram of it warms more slowly when the same heat is supplied.
The 200 g water has fewer hydrogen bonds per gram, so less of the heat it receives is used to warm it up.
The slope of a line depends on how many points are plotted, and both lines were given six points each.

why.correct: Specific heat is per gram. With equal heat input per minute, doubling the mass halves the temperature rise per minute: 6 °C/min becomes about 3 °C/min.
options: Correct: same heat in, twice the grams to warm.
Specific heat is a property of water per gram; it is the same in both beakers.
Water has the same hydrogen bonding per gram whatever the amount.
Slope depends on rise and run, not on the number of points.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data for the tube with enzyme?
options: Monomer mass rose quickly at first, then rose more and more slowly and leveled off near 50 mg.
Monomer mass rose by the same amount in each 2-minute interval until the end of the run.
Monomer mass rose slowly at first, then rose faster and faster as the run went on.
Monomer mass rose to a peak at 8 minutes and then began to fall as monomers were joined again.

why.correct: Increases per 2 minutes: 18, 16, 10, 5, 1 mg. The curve is steep at first and flattens as it approaches 50 mg.
options: Correct: the increments shrink and the curve plateaus.
The increments shrink from 18 mg to 1 mg; they are not equal.
This is the reverse of the pattern: the biggest increases come first.
The mass never falls: 49 mg at 8 min, 50 mg at 10 min.

items.q: Calculate the slope of the enzyme curve between 0 and 4 minutes, in mg of monomer per minute, to one decimal place.
Which is the best explanation for why the enzyme curve levels off near 50 mg?
options: The tube started with 50 mg of polymer, so once nearly all of it is broken into monomers there is little left to release.
The enzyme is used up after each reaction it speeds up, so by 10 minutes there is no enzyme left in the tube to break bonds.
Water molecules are used up after 6 minutes, so hydrolysis stops because nothing is left to add across bonds.
The monomers start joining back together by hydrolysis, which balances the breakdown after about 8 minutes.

why.correct: The maximum possible product is set by the polymer available: 50 mg of polymer can release at most about 50 mg of monomers (a little more, because each hydrolysis adds the mass of a water molecule). As the polymer runs out, each interval releases less.
options: Correct: the curve approaches the total amount available.
Each enzyme molecule comes out of the reaction unchanged and can act again and again.
The polymer is dissolved in water, so water is in huge excess and does not run out.
Joining monomers removes water (dehydration synthesis); hydrolysis is the breaking reaction.

items.q: What is the purpose of the tube that received water instead of enzyme?
options: It shows how much monomer is released without the enzyme, so the enzyme's effect can be measured against it.
It keeps the volume in both tubes the same, which is its main role in the experiment that was run.
It shows how fast water by itself breaks the enzyme down, so the enzyme dose can be corrected.
It provides extra monomers that the enzyme in the other tube can use to build the polymer again.

why.correct: It is the control group: everything matches except the enzyme. The small slow rise (2.5 mg in 10 min) is the baseline the enzyme curve is compared with.
options: Correct: a baseline for comparison.
Matching volume is part of good design, but the tube's main job is to show the result with no enzyme.
The water tube has no enzyme in it, so it cannot show the enzyme breaking down.
The tubes are separate; nothing passes from one to the other.

items.q: A student measured how much monomer four different enzymes (A, B, C and D) each released from the same polymer in 10 minutes. Which graph type best displays the results?
options: Bar graph, one bar per enzyme
Line graph, joining the four enzymes in order
Histogram of the four masses of monomer released
Scatterplot of enzyme letter against mass released

why.correct: The independent variable (enzyme type) is categorical: there is nothing "between" enzyme A and enzyme B. Separate bars compare categories.
options: Correct: categories become separate bars.
A line implies values between the points, which do not exist for categories.
A histogram shows how often values fall in ranges of one variable; it does not compare named groups.
A scatterplot needs two measured numbers; enzyme identity is a category, not a number.

items.q: A student plans a graph of water temperature (°C) every 30 seconds while a beaker is heated. Select ALL the choices that are correct for this graph.
options: Temperature on the x-axis and time on the y-axis
A line graph, because time is continuous
A bar for each reading, because each reading is a separate category
Axis scales that start at the first and last values recorded, spaced by the readings
Each axis labeled with the quantity and its unit, for example "Time (s)"

why.correct: Time is the independent variable (x-axis), it is continuous (line graph), and each axis needs a label with units. Scales must be evenly spaced numbers, not just the recorded values.
options: Reversed: time is set by the student (independent, x-axis) and temperature is measured (dependent, y-axis).
Correct: a continuous independent variable suits a line graph.
Readings at different times are points along a continuous scale, not categories.
A scale must be even (for example every 30 s); marking only recorded values can make the spacing uneven.
Correct: a label and a unit on each axis.

items.q: Across 40 lakes, lakes with more plant growth along the shore also had warmer surface water. A student concludes that plant growth warms lakes. What is the best response?
options: The data show a correlation; a third factor, such as more sunlight on shallow lakes, could raise both, so an experiment is needed.
The conclusion is correct, because a strong positive correlation between two measured variables shows that the first variable causes the second one.
The conclusion is backward: the data prove that warm water causes plant growth, since temperature is measured in °C.
The data are useless, because a study of lakes has no independent variable and so it is unable to show a relationship of any kind.

why.correct: A correlation means two variables change together. It does not show which (if either) causes the other; another factor can drive both. Testing causation needs a controlled experiment in which one factor is changed and others are held constant.
options: Correct: correlation, possible third factor, test with an experiment.
Correlation does not establish causation.
The data do not prove either direction; the units of a variable say nothing about cause.
Observational data can show a relationship (a correlation); they just cannot by themselves show cause.

items.q: On a scatterplot of mass of water (g) against time to boil (min) for 12 beakers, the points rise from lower left to upper right and lie close to a straight trend line. What does this show?
options: A strong positive correlation: beakers with more water tended to take longer to boil.
A strong negative correlation: beakers with more water tended to boil sooner.
No correlation, because the points do not touch the trend line exactly.
Each beaker took the same time to boil, because the points form a straight line.

why.correct: Points rising left to right show a positive correlation; points close to the trend line show a strong one.
options: Correct.
A negative correlation would slope down from upper left to lower right.
A trend line summarizes the pattern; points cluster around it without touching it exactly.
A rising line means boiling time increases with mass, not that it is constant.

items.q: A student's y-axis for temperature is marked 20, 25, 35, 40, 60 °C at equal spacing, one mark for each reading she took. What is wrong, and what does it do to the graph?
options: The scale is uneven, so equal distances stand for different temperature changes and the shape of the curve is distorted.
Nothing is wrong, because each recorded value appears on the axis, so a reader can find the exact temperature of each point.
The scale should start at 0 °C; any axis that starts above zero is an error.
The temperatures should be on the x-axis, because they are the numbers that were recorded.

why.correct: Equal spacing must mean equal steps (for example every 10 °C). Here one gap is 5 °C and another 20 °C, so a steady warming would look bumpy and slopes cannot be compared.
options: Correct: an uneven scale distorts the curve.
Showing the recorded values does not make up for a scale whose steps are unequal.
An axis may start above zero if it is labeled clearly and the scale is even.
Temperature is the measured response here, so it belongs on the y-axis.

items.q: A student measures the mass of 60 seeds and wants to show how many seeds fall in each 0.1 g range. Which graph type is this?
options: Histogram
Line graph
Scatterplot
Pie chart of seed masses

why.correct: A histogram shows how often values of one variable fall into each range (bin).
options: Correct.
A line graph shows change along a continuous independent variable.
A scatterplot pairs two measured variables for each individual.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole and does not show a distribution over ranges.

items.q: Put the steps for building a graph from a data table in order.
options: Decide which variable is independent and which is dependent.
Choose the graph type from the kind of independent variable.
Draw and label the axes with quantities and units, using even scales that fit the data.
Plot the points or bars for each group.
Add a key for the groups and a title, and draw a trend line if one is needed.

why.correct: Variables decide the axes and the graph type; axes and scales come before plotting; the key, title and trend line finish the graph.

items.q: A trend line on a graph of monomer released (mg) against time (min) passes through (3, 14) and (9, 41). Calculate its slope in mg per minute, to one decimal place.

why.correct: Slope = (41 − 14) mg ÷ (9 − 3) min = 27 ÷ 6 = 4.5 mg/min. Use two points on the line, not data points off it.
